author: David
message: I agree. Not everything has to be purely pragmatic. Creating games or writing new songs don't necessarily fix a "problem." But think that sometimes people don't always use the word "problem" to mean "something that needs to be fixed" when they say "what problem are you trying to solve?" Maybe they just mean "What is the purpose of this ____?"

author: Paul Daigle
message:
I guess I don't see the attitude that you describe as particularly practical, or even pragmatic. Investing in basic science and theory is like playing a lottery that we're guaranteed to win, and it does sove problems. Cloning the wooly mammoth does solve a very real problem, namely, there are no wooly mammoths. If we decide not to solve that problem, then we won't learn all the things about how things work that we need to learn in order to clone a wooly mammoth. We don't know, as a society, what the value of learning those things will be, but historically science has had excellent ROI so it's a safe bet that we'll gain more than we lose from the totality of basic biological research. Ditto space research, sending stuff to mars, etc.

What people mean when they talk about "solving our problems here on earth" is invariably putting big expensive band-aids on big obvious wounds. This is a laudable endeavor, and possibly even a desirable one, but it ignores the very real problem of finding out why we have big obvious wounds and how we can make that stop happening. Learning about that latter thing is the realm of basic science, art, games, and theory.

author: Sean Chen
message:
Hi Dan, I just found your blog recently, but I've read through a good chunk of your posts already. I love your writing; it's very clean and no-nonsense-y and yet it's also very descriptive. You come off as incredibly intelligent and well-read, and I really appreciate that in your blog.

I'm an aspiring software developer myself, having just jumped in to the world of programming. Coming from a math background myself though, your post resonates with me a bit. Math is one of those subjects that pushes its own boundaries for its own sake (if that makes any sense). Branches of math like topology, number theory, category theory, etc., were devised centuries ago for no other reason than because the mathematicians who dreamed them up were trying to solve some other almost equally abstract math problem.

There's lots of math out there that isn't obviously applicable to any real world problems right now, but I believe that eventually every branch and aspect of math will become applicable in the future; we're just not there yet. Topology, which was 'invented' in the eighteenth century, had very few practical applications back then. Now it is being applied widely in the fields of computer science and physics. As technology increases, we're able to discover new ways of harnessing mathematical concepts and ideas that were generated centuries ago. And new math research is pushing the boundaries of our mathematical understanding every day!

Anyways, sorry about the random blurb. Keep up the awesome work with your blog; I look forward to your upcoming posts!
